nameStory: The 'shingled' part of this lichen's name comes from its overlapping, tile-like lobes that look remarkably like roof shingles arranged on a rock surface. The 'camouflage' refers to how perfectly it blends with weathered granite and other light-colored rocks, making it nearly invisible until you know what to look for.
description: Shingled Camouflage Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms tight, overlapping patches on rocks, creating a distinctive shingle-like pattern. The individual lobes are small and closely pressed to the rock surface, giving it an almost scaly appearance. It typically forms patches several inches across, though old specimens can cover much larger areas. This rock-dwelling lichen has mastered the art of blending in with its stone substrate.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms tight, overlapping lobes that lie flat against rock surfaces like tiny roof shingles, creating a distinctive scaled or tiled pattern

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish to brownish when dry, becoming more vibrant and slightly greenish when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found exclusively on rocks, particularly granite and other acidic stone surfaces exposed to weather

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and papery when dry, with lobes that are firmly attached and don't easily peel away from the rock

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are quite small, typically less than half an inch across, but colonies can spread across several inches of rock surface

habitat: Look for this lichen on exposed granite outcrops, stone walls, and weathered boulders throughout New England's mountains and rocky areas. It prefers acidic rock surfaces that receive good light but aren't constantly wet. You're most likely to spot it on south-facing rock faces and old stone foundations in areas with clean air.

seasonality.spring: More vibrant and noticeable after spring rains when it takes on a subtle greenish tint. The overlapping pattern becomes more pronounced when wet.
seasonality.summer: Often appears quite dry and pale, blending seamlessly with sun-bleached rock surfaces. Best observed in early morning when dew brings out its colors.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture makes it more visible again, and the shingle pattern stands out nicely against colorful fallen leaves that may accumulate around rocks.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow, and winter's clear air often provides the best viewing conditions. Ice and snow highlight the textural differences between lichen and bare rock.

funFact: This lichen is so perfectly camouflaged that rock climbers often grab handholds covered in it without ever noticing it's there - they're literally gripping a living organism that might be decades or even centuries old!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, gray foliose lichens on rocks, but the distinctive shingled, overlapping pattern is unique - think 'tiny roof tiles' and you'll remember the key feature that sets it apart from other rock lichens.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's common, this lichen has been recorded only once in New England, making it quite rare in our region. If you think you've found it, consider taking photos and reporting your observation to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Since this is the only Montanelia species recorded in New England, compare it with other small foliose rock lichens in the shield lichen family. Unlike smoother rock lichens, Shingled Camouflage Lichen has that distinctive overlapping, scaled texture that looks remarkably organized and geometric. Other rock lichens tend to have more random, irregular lobe patterns rather than this neat, shingle-like arrangement.
